title: Wisdom as practice
hookLine: the sixth: seeing things as they are, in every act

lines: A GIFT CAN BE GIVEN TO SHOW OFF.
WHAT TURNS IT INTO THE REAL THING?
cards: A coin, a bowl of rice, an hour of your time handed to someone who needs it. That's giving, the first perfection. But a gift can be given to show off.
A precept can be kept with a sneer at the people who don't keep it. Patience can be gritted teeth, effort can be pride, and even a quiet mind can be one more thing to own.

Something has to turn each of these into the real thing. In the Mahayana list, that something comes last, as the sixth, and the other five lean on it. You met the short sutra named for it early on the path.

teach.b: The Sanskrit word is prajna, in Pali panna: wisdom, understanding, the mind that sees. In the old suttas, the phrase that goes with it is seeing things as they really are. And what is that?
The Dhammapada puts it in three short verses: all conditioned things pass away; all conditioned things are suffering, unable to fully satisfy; all things are without a self.
When a person sees this with wisdom, the verses say, they grow weary of suffering, and that is the path to purity. So wisdom here isn't knowing lots of facts.
It's seeing, right in the middle of a moment, that this too is changing, this too can't hold me up forever, and this too is not a solid me. Now the Mahayana turn.
A whole family of sutras is named for this perfection: prajnaparamita, the perfection of wisdom. The short Heart Sutra belongs to it.

teach.h: THE GUIDE WHO LEADS THE BLIND.
teach.b: Some of these texts compare the first five perfections to people who cannot see, and wisdom to the guide who leads them to the city. Without it, giving is just handing things over.
With it, the giver sees no solid giver, no solid gift, no solid receiver to cling to, and gives freely anyway.
So wisdom isn't a sixth task added at the end of the list. It's the light the other five are done by: giving, keeping precepts, patience, effort and sitting, each one done with the eyes open.

how: Mahayana Buddhists count wisdom (prajna) as the sixth perfection and chant texts like the Heart Sutra from the perfection of wisdom sutras; in Theravada, wisdom (panna) is developed by seeing impermanence, unsatisfactoriness and not-self in daily experience.

o: seeing things as they are: changing, unsatisfying, not a self
a clever mind that wins arguments about what is true
knowing a great many facts and texts about the Buddha's teaching

games.q: you give a gift, keep a precept, sit an hour. what turns each of these into a perfection, in the Mahayana view?
o: doing them with wisdom, seeing things as they are.
games.why: some perfection of wisdom texts call the first five like people who can't see, and wisdom the guide that leads them.

practice: Choose something small in front of you, a cup, your hand, the light on a wall, and look at it for a few breaths, as it is.
Notice that it's changing, even slowly, and can't stay exactly like this; then turn the same gentle look on a feeling you have right now, restlessness or ease, which is changing too.
No need to think hard; just see it, and let the seeing be enough.

wordCard.voice: Wisdom as practice. Prajna, the sixth perfection: seeing things as they are, the light every other perfection is done by. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit prajna (Pali panna): wisdom, understanding; the sixth perfection, and the root of prajnaparamita, the perfection of wisdom.

carryVoice: Your line: the sixth perfection. This is changing: three words that fit in the middle of washing up or waiting in line. Six perfections, all here.

sources.ref: Astasahasrika Prajnaparamita (perfection of wisdom in 8,000 lines), the simile of the blind and the guide
